title: Chapter 11: State Legislature – Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council

blocks.content: The Parliament can abolish a Legislative Council where it exists or create it where it does not exist, if the Legislative Assembly of the concerned state passes a resolution to that effect by a special majority.

rows: Permanent body (1/3rd members retire every 2 years)
Exclusive power to introduce and pass
Can only delay up to 14 days without amendments

items: Currently, only six states possess a bicameral legislature: Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana.
Unlike the Rajya Sabha at the Union level, the Legislative Council can be completely abolished by Parliament under Article 169.
In the case of Money Bills, the Legislative Council has virtually no powers and can withhold the bill for a maximum period of 14 days only.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The State Legislature consists of the Governor and the Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha), plus the Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) in bicameral states.
Under Article 169, Parliament can create or abolish a Legislative Council if the State Assembly passes a resolution by a special majority.
The Legislative Assembly is directly elected by the people, having a maximum strength of 500 and a minimum strength of 60, subject to constitutional exceptions.
The Legislative Council is a permanent body not subject to dissolution, with one-third of its members retiring every two years.
The maximum strength of the Legislative Council is fixed at one-third of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly, with a constitutional minimum of 40.
